name: Anglo-Frisian
region: The Frisian coast of the North Sea; lowland Britain
defining_innovation: Anglo-Frisian brightening: West Germanic *a fronted to æ (Old English dæg, Old Frisian dei, against Old Saxon dag), together with palatalisation of *k before front vowels.

chapters.title: Origins
chapters.body:
English and Frisian are each other's closest relatives. The traditional explanation is that both come from dialects spoken along the southern North Sea coast, roughly from the northern Netherlands to Jutland, in the first centuries CE. There they went through a set of sound changes that their continental neighbours did not share.

Frisian is attested late: the earliest substantial Old Frisian texts are law codes from the 13th century. Much of the comparison with Old English therefore has to see through centuries of separate development.

chapters.title: Brightening and Palatalisation
chapters.body:
Two changes give Anglo-Frisian its character. The first, **brightening**, fronted West Germanic `*a` to `æ` in most environments. Old English has *dæg* 'day' and Old Frisian *dei*, against Old Saxon and Old High German *dag*/*tag*. In Old English the `a` was later restored before a back vowel in the next syllable, giving singular *dæg* but plural *dagas*.

The second, **palatalisation**, turned `k` and `g` into sounds made further forward in the mouth when they stood next to front vowels. Old English *ċīese* 'cheese' (from Latin *caseus*) and *ċiriċe* 'church' had `[tʃ]`, and *ġeolu* 'yellow' had `[j]`. Modern West Frisian *tsjerke* 'church' shows the same kind of development, while Dutch keeps *kerk*. Scots *kirk* and English *dike* beside *ditch* are among the doublets that Norse contact left behind.

These two changes sit alongside the older **nasal spirant law** shared with Old Saxon. It explains why English has *goose*, *us*, *mouth*, *five* where German has *Gans*, *uns*, *Mund*, *fünf*.

chapters.title: Across the Sea
chapters.body:
In the 5th and 6th centuries, speakers of these coastal dialects settled in lowland Britain. Bede, writing around 731, names them as Angles, Saxons and Jutes. Old English and Old Frisian became separate languages when they were divided by sea. How many people moved, and how much of the British population shifted language instead of being replaced, is still debated by historians, archaeologists and geneticists.

In Britain, Old English developed rich literary traditions in several dialects (Northumbrian, Mercian, Kentish and West Saxon). The Frisians remained on the continental coast and lost ground over the centuries to Low German and Dutch.

chapters.title: Daughter Branches
chapters.body: Once the sea divided them, the two halves went separate ways. **Anglic** (Old English, and from it English and Scots) was reshaped by Norse and French contact and spread worldwide. **Frisian** stayed on the continental coast, lost ground over the centuries to Dutch and Low German, and survives as three small languages.

speakers.note: Almost all English; the Frisian languages together have well under half a million speakers.

sources.citation: Eberhard, David M., Gary F. Simons & Charles D. Fennig (eds.). 2024. Ethnologue: Languages of the World. 27th ed. Dallas: SIL International.
Moseley, Christopher (ed.). 2010. Atlas of the World's Languages in Danger. 3rd ed. Paris: UNESCO Publishing.

turning_points.title: Coastal dialects diverge
turning_points.description: The dialects along the North Sea coast develop their own innovations and separate from the rest of West Germanic. Whether English and Frisian share one ancestor after that point, or only grew alike as neighbours, is debated.

sources.citation: Nielsen, Hans Frede. 1989. The Germanic Languages: Origins and Early Dialectal Interrelations. Tuscaloosa: University of Alabama Press.
Stiles, Patrick V. 1995. Remarks on the 'Anglo-Frisian' thesis. In Friesische Studien II (NOWELE Supplement 12). Odense: Odense University Press.

turning_points.title: Nasal spirant law
turning_points.description: A nasal is lost before a fricative and the vowel is lengthened: `*gans` → Old English *gōs* 'goose', `*uns` → *ūs*, `*munþ` → *mūþ* 'mouth', `*fimf` → *fīf*. Old Saxon shares the change, so it is a North Sea feature and not exclusively Anglo-Frisian.

sources.citation: Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.title: Anglo-Frisian brightening
turning_points.description: West Germanic `*a` is fronted to `æ` in most environments: Old English *dæg*, Old Frisian *dei* 'day', against Old Saxon *dag*. In Old English it was later partly reversed before back vowels (plural *dagas*).

sources.citation: Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.
Fulk, R. D. 2018. A Comparative Grammar of the Early Germanic Languages. Amsterdam: John Benjamins.

turning_points.title: Palatalisation of k and g
turning_points.description: Next to front vowels, `k` became `[tʃ]` and `g` became `[j]`: Old English *ċiriċe* 'church', *ġeolu* 'yellow', West Frisian *tsjerke*. The English and Frisian outcomes differ in detail and chronology, and scholars dispute whether this is one shared change or two parallel ones.

sources.citation: Stiles, Patrick V. 1995. Remarks on the 'Anglo-Frisian' thesis. In Friesische Studien II (NOWELE Supplement 12). Odense: Odense University Press.
Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

turning_points.notation: k ɡ → tʃ j / next to front vowels

turning_points.title: Settlement of Britain
turning_points.description: Coastal Germanic speakers settle lowland Britain, and Old English and Old Frisian become separate languages. The scale of the migration, and how much of the British population shifted language instead, are debated.

sources.citation: Bede. c. 731. Historia ecclesiastica gentis Anglorum, I.15.
Ringe, Don & Ann Taylor. 2014. The Development of Old English. Oxford: Oxford University Press.

contested_classifications.proposed_grouping: Anglo-Frisian as a genetic subgroup: English and Frisian descend from one ancestor within West Germanic
contested_classifications.evidence_for: English and Frisian share brightening of `*a` to `æ`, palatalisation of `k` and `g` next to front vowels, and further vowel developments not found together anywhere else in West Germanic. The handbook tree has long placed them together on that basis.
contested_classifications.evidence_against: Stiles (1995) and others argue that many of the shared features are either found in Old Saxon too, and so belong to a wider North Sea zone, or took place separately in English and Frisian after they had parted. On this reading the resemblance comes from long coastal contact, not a single ancestor. This app draws Anglo-Frisian as a node, following the conventional tree, but the node itself is part of the debate.

sources.citation: Stiles, Patrick V. 1995. Remarks on the 'Anglo-Frisian' thesis. In Friesische Studien II (NOWELE Supplement 12). Odense: Odense University Press.
Nielsen, Hans Frede. 1989. The Germanic Languages: Origins and Early Dialectal Interrelations. Tuscaloosa: University of Alabama Press.
